name: Meta Platforms

summary.text: Meta Platforms (formerly Facebook, Inc.) owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. Founder Mark Zuckerberg controls a majority of shareholder voting power through high-vote Class B stock. In 2019 the FTC imposed a $5 billion penalty on Facebook over privacy violations. In December 2020 the FTC and a coalition of 48 state and territorial attorneys general filed separate antitrust suits over its acquisitions of Instagram and WhatsApp. In November 2025 a federal judge ruled that the FTC had not shown Meta currently holds monopoly power; the FTC has appealed.

facts.claim: On December 9, 2020, the FTC sued Facebook, alleging it illegally maintained a monopoly in personal social networking, partly by acquiring Instagram (2012) and WhatsApp (2014). That same day a bipartisan coalition of 48 attorneys general, led by New York, filed a separate antitrust suit. In November 2025, Judge James Boasberg ruled that the FTC had not shown Meta currently holds monopoly power.

facts.claim: The USPTO issued US patent 12,513,102 B2, 'Simulation of a user of a social networking system using a language model', to Meta Platforms Technologies LLC on December 30, 2025; the application (18/523,545) was filed November 29, 2023 and names CTO Andrew Garrod Bosworth as inventor.

facts.claim: The patent's abstract states that a language model trained on a user's interactions may simulate the user when absent from the social networking system, for example during a long break or if the user is deceased.
facts.quote: The language model may be used for simulating the user when the user is absent from the social networking system, for example, when the user takes a long break or if the user is deceased

facts.claim: Meta's Community Standards memorialization policy adds 'Remembering' above a deceased user's name, blocks logins and aims to preserve the account without changes; since 2015 users can name a legacy contact or opt for deletion on death.
facts.quote: to respect the choices someone made while alive, we aim to preserve their account without changes after they pass away

facts.claim: On July 24, 2019 the FTC announced that Facebook agreed to pay a $5 billion penalty to settle charges that it violated the Commission's 2012 order by deceiving users about their ability to control the privacy of their personal information. The FTC described the penalty as the largest ever imposed on any company for violating consumers' privacy.
facts.quote: largest ever imposed on any company for violating consumers' privacy

sources.title: FTC Imposes $5 Billion Penalty and Sweeping New Privacy Restrictions on Facebook
Fact Sheet on 2019 FTC Order with Facebook

facts.claim: The 2019 FTC order requires Facebook's board to designate an Independent Privacy Committee from which Facebook officers and employees, including Mark Zuckerberg, are disqualified; the committee is briefed on material privacy risks and has approval and removal authority over designated compliance officers and the third-party assessor. The order also requires a program to monitor third-party developers and to terminate access for developers that break the rules, and clear notice and express consent before any materially different use of facial recognition.
facts.quote: Facebook officers and employees, including Mr. Zuckerberg, are disqualified from membership.

sources.title: Fact Sheet on 2019 FTC Order with Facebook
FTC Imposes $5 Billion Penalty and Sweeping New Privacy Restrictions on Facebook

facts.claim: Under the 2019 FTC order, Mark Zuckerberg must certify quarterly, under threat of civil and criminal penalties, that Facebook's privacy program complies with the order. FTC Chairman Simons said the $5 billion penalty equalled about 9% of Facebook's 2018 revenue and about 23% of its 2018 profit; Commissioner Slaughter dissented, arguing the sum was substantially less significant relative to Facebook's finances.
facts.quote: certifying quarterly, under threat of civil and criminal penalties, that the company's privacy program is in compliance with the Order

facts.claim: Facebook's Form 8-K exhibit of July 24, 2019 reported the $5.0 billion FTC penalty and stated that the company would regularly certify its compliance with the privacy program to the FTC.

facts.claim: On July 24, 2019 the SEC filed a complaint against Facebook and announced that Facebook agreed to pay $100 million to settle charges that, from 2016 until mid-March 2018, it presented the risk of misuse of user data as merely hypothetical, although the SEC said Facebook knew by December 2015 that a researcher had improperly sold information on tens of millions of users to Cambridge Analytica.
facts.quote: Facebook discovered the misuse of its users' information in 2015, but did not correct its existing disclosure for more than two years

sources.title: Facebook to Pay $100 Million for Misleading Investors About the Risks It Faced From Misuse of User Data (Press Release 2019-140)

facts.claim: The SEC's $100 million Facebook penalty was placed in a Fair Fund; a 2022 distribution plan provides for paying the fund, plus interest and less taxes and costs, to investors who purchased or acquired Facebook common stock from January 28, 2016 through March 19, 2018.
facts.quote: to investors who purchased or acquired Facebook common stock from January 28, 2016 through March 19, 2018

sources.title: Distribution Plan, SEC v. Facebook, Inc. Fair Fund

facts.claim: In an April 4, 2018 Newsroom post by chief technology officer Mike Schroepfer, Facebook said the information of up to 87 million people, mostly in the US, may have been improperly shared with Cambridge Analytica, and announced restrictions on the Pages API, Facebook Login permissions, inactive apps and other data access. The figure previously reported was 50 million; Cambridge Analytica said it had licensed data for no more than 30 million people.
facts.quote: the Facebook information of up to 87 million people — mostly in the US — may have been improperly shared with Cambridge Analytica

sources.title: An Update on Our Plans to Restrict Data Access on Facebook
Facebook Says Cambridge Analytica Data Grab May Be Much Bigger Than First Reported

facts.claim: Mark Zuckerberg was the sole witness at an April 10, 2018 joint hearing of the Senate Judiciary and Commerce Committees. His written testimony said about 300,000 people installed the app that gathered data, that this access extended to information about tens of millions of their friends, and, of Facebook's failures, 'It was my mistake, and I'm sorry.'
facts.quote: It was my mistake, and I'm sorry.

facts.claim: Facebook COO Sheryl Sandberg said on NBC's Today show in April 2018 that after receiving legal assurances in 2015 that Cambridge Analytica had deleted improperly obtained data, the company should have audited the firm: 'What we didn't do is the next step of an audit and we're trying to that now.' The AP reported that the audit was on hold in deference to a UK investigation.
facts.quote: What we didn't do is the next step of an audit and we're trying to that now

sources.title: Facebook says it should have audited Cambridge Analytica

facts.claim: On October 10, 2023 Judge Vince Chhabria of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California granted final approval to a $725 million settlement in In re Facebook, Inc. Consumer Privacy User Profile Litigation, a class action prompted by the March 2018 reports that Cambridge Analytica had harvested information from up to 87 million Facebook users. Plaintiffs' attorneys described it as the largest data-privacy class action recovery to date.
facts.quote: the largest data-privacy class action recovery to date

sources.title: Facebook's $725 Million Cambridge Analytica Deal Gets Final OK
Judge approves $725 million deal in Meta data privacy class action

facts.claim: In December 2018 District of Columbia Attorney General Karl Racine sued Facebook under the District's Consumer Protection Procedures Act, alleging it misled users about how well their data was protected and failed for years to monitor third-party apps; his office said the data of more than 340,000 District residents was exposed. In 2019 the D.C. Superior Court denied Facebook's motion to dismiss, and later denied a second attempt. These are allegations in a lawsuit, not findings.
facts.quote: monetary and injunctive relief, including relief for harmed consumers, damages, and penalties to the District

facts.claim: In May 2022 the D.C. Attorney General filed a separate suit naming Mark Zuckerberg personally, alleging that Facebook and Zuckerberg violated the Consumer Protection Procedures Act by knowingly giving third parties such as Cambridge Analytica access to the information of millions of users, including 340,000 D.C. residents. This is an allegation in a complaint.
facts.quote: Facebook and Zuckerberg knowingly gave third-party companies like Cambridge Analytica access to the information of millions, including 340,000 Washington D.C. residents

connections.claim: Peter Thiel made Facebook's first outside investment, putting in $500,000 in 2004 at a $5 million valuation. He served on its board from April 2005 until Meta's 2022 annual meeting.

openQuestions: The 2023 'Project Lazarus' 4chan claim and the December 2025 patent are recorded separately; no source establishes a link between them.

The outcome of the D.C. Attorney General's 2018 suit against Facebook and the 2022 suit against Zuckerberg (judgment, settlement or dismissal) should be checked on the D.C. Superior Court docket; only the denied motions to dismiss were found.
A law firm's page says the Ninth Circuit affirmed the $725 million settlement approval on February 13, 2025; confirm from the court's opinion before use.
